caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Lesotho's debt is driven by SACU revenue volatility and chronic political instability that has interrupted fiscal discipline. From 33.8% of GDP in 2010, the series low, the ratio climbed to 64.4% in 2022, the series high, as SACU transfers fell and COVID forced borrowing, before easing to a projected 49.3% in 2025. The Lesotho Highlands Water Project Phase II, financed partly by borrowing, is the big capital item. Debt is mostly concessional and domestic, so sustainability is manageable, but the pattern is concerning: every SACU downturn ratchets the ratio up, and it never fully comes back down.
inflation_management: Lesotho's inflation is imported from South Africa through the loti's one-to-one peg to the rand under the Common Monetary Area. It peaked at 10.7% in the 2008 commodity boom and troughed at 3.3% in 2010, tracking South African inflation closely ever since: 8.2% in 2022 during the global shock, easing to a projected 4.4% in 2025. The Central Bank of Lesotho shadows South African Reserve Bank policy, so there is no independent monetary lever; inflation management is effectively outsourced. The peg has delivered reasonable price stability, but it also means Lesotho cannot use monetary policy to offset its frequent fiscal and political shocks.

key_events.event: Global commodity boom pushed inflation to 10.7%, the series high.
Political crisis: prime minister fled amid an alleged coup attempt; SADC mediation followed.
Years of coalition instability interrupted IMF programs and fiscal consolidation.
COVID-19 and SACU revenue collapse pushed debt to 64.4% of GDP, the series high.
Sam Matekane's Revolution for Prosperity won the 2022 election, promising economic reform.
Lesotho Highlands Water Project Phase II advanced, promising future water royalties from South Africa.

outlook_next_decade: The base case is continued SACU-dependent volatility with inflation anchored by the rand peg and debt near 50% of GDP. Upside comes from water royalties, textiles under AGOA (if renewed), and political stability under Matekane; downside is another SACU slump or political crisis forcing a debt spike. Uncertainty is moderate: the macro framework is sound, but Lesotho's politics have repeatedly been the binding constraint.
